title: Creating the Home-Field Advantage
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Sports research shows that home-field advantage is real and significant—home teams win up to 10% more often—but COVID-era games without spectators revealed that the advantage nearly disappears without fans. Fan support, not field familiarity, is the primary driver. Leaders can deliberately create the same dynamic in organizations by turning stakeholders (customers, family members, colleagues, board members, alumni) into active supporters. Unlike in sports, workplace fans must be explicitly invited—the stands don't fill themselves. Once built, the fan base becomes a genuine source of team energy and momentum, not merely a backdrop to performance.
points: Games played without fans during COVID showed the home-field advantage nearly vanished—confirming that crowd support, not field familiarity, is the primary driver.
Leaders can create a workplace equivalent by deliberately inviting stakeholders (customers, families, colleagues, alumni) to become visible supporters of the team.
Unlike in sports, workplace supporters must be explicitly recruited—the stands don't fill themselves, and too many leaders miss this.
The fan base is built one invitation at a time; each new supporter added to the circle expands the reservoir of energy available to the team.
Once a community of supporters exists, the leader's job is to remind the team those supporters are there—making the home-field effect conscious and motivating.
quotes: In nearly every sport, home teams enjoy an edge, winning up to 10 percent more often than their visiting opponents.
Games played without spectators, as occurred during parts of the COVID-19 pandemic, showed that the home advantage almost disappeared when no one was in the bleachers cheering the team on.
The lesson is clear: Performance follows support, not the other way around.
Just as a roaring crowd can lift a home team beyond its normal capabilities, leaders who cultivate genuine believers give their teams access to a similar reservoir of energy.
But unlike in sports, stakeholders must be invited to become fans. Too many leaders miss this. In the workplace, the stands don’t fill themselves.
The fan base is built one invitation at a time by leaders who understand that support is not a backdrop to performance but a source of it.
